title: Zero-error query complexity of recursive majority-of-three
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
Determine, up to multiplicative constants independent of the height \(h\), the zero-error randomized query complexity \(Q(h)\) of the complete height-\(h\) recursive majority-of-three function \(M_h\).

Set \(M_0(x)=x\). For \(h\ge0\), divide an input of length \(3^{h+1}\) into three consecutive blocks \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},x^{(3)}\) of length \(3^h\) and define
\[M_{h+1}(x)=\operatorname{Maj}_3\bigl(M_h(x^{(1)}),M_h(x^{(2)}),M_h(x^{(3)})\bigr),\]
where \(\operatorname{Maj}_3(a,b,c)=1\) exactly when at least two of its three Boolean arguments are one.

An algorithm adaptively queries individual input bits and must always output the correct value. Its cost is the maximum over inputs of its expected number of queries, with expectation only over its internal randomness. If \(\mathcal T_h\) is the finite set of deterministic decision trees computing \(M_h\) without repeating a query on a path, then
\[Q(h)=\min_{\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal T_h)}\ \max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{3^h}}\ \mathbb E_{T\sim\mu}\bigl[q_T(x)\bigr].\]
Here \(q_T(x)\) is the number of queried bits on the input path, and \(\Delta(\mathcal T_h)\) is the set of probability distributions on these trees. The target is matching upper and lower bounds for this full function as \(h\to\infty\), including any nonconstant factors beyond its exponential growth rate.
why: Determining this complexity would explain the full power of random adaptive evaluation on one of the simplest recursively defined Boolean functions. It is a canonical setting where exact computation gains substantially from randomization, but the best possible savings are still not understood despite decades of improved bounds.
status_note: Source-open in O’Donnell’s Example 8.64 and still explicitly unresolved in §1.2 of Al-Dhalaan–Ben-David, arXiv:2601.08073v1, submitted 12 January 2026. On 16 September 2026 the original zero-error definition, the 2015/2016 quantitative bounds, the Göös–Jayram improvement, and the 2026 composition-limit statement were read. The 2026 result equates the bounded-error and zero-error exponential rates without determining their value, so it does not resolve this stronger constant-factor asymptotic target. Bounded later-work searches found no matching resolution. This status distinguishes the checked statements from an independent verification of all their proofs or an exhaustive literature search.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Definition 8.61 specifies zero-error randomization and worst-input expected cost. Example 8.64 explicitly records the unresolved recursive-majority complexity question.
Magniez and coauthors establish the stated 2.64944-base zero-error upper bound and a 2.57143-base lower bound, improving previous work.
Göös and Jayram improve the lower bound to a base exceeding 2.59, with the more precise value and parameter loss stated in their discussion of Theorem 2.2.

Al-Dhalaan and Ben-David give equality of zero-error and bounded-error composition limits for this function and explicitly retain their unknown value. The author version’s model, theorem and open-status passage were checked; its full proof was not independently reverified.

importance.reason: A longstanding benchmark problem in randomized query complexity, with a simple complete specification, nontrivial adaptive behavior and connections to composition and communication complexity. The remaining gap concerns the intrinsic cost of unrestricted exact algorithms, rather than a technical constant in one prescribed procedure.

sentences: Recursive majority-of-three evaluates a complete ternary tree whose internal nodes take majority votes.
An algorithm may adaptively inspect leaf bits in any order, but it must always return the exact root value.
The cost is its largest expected number of queries over all possible inputs.
The task is to determine that optimum as the tree grows, with upper and lower bounds matching up to constant factors.
Known lower and upper exponential rates remain different, and a 2026 equality between composition limits does not determine the optimum.

definitions:
The input domain is all bit strings of length \(n=3^h\), with \(h\) any nonnegative integer. Equivalently, bits label the leaves of a known, complete ternary tree, every internal node applies majority to its three children, and the requested output is the root value. The tree shape and the height are known to the algorithm. There is no promise on leaf values, no random input distribution and no promise that a subtree is close to a tie. Recursive majority is not ordinary majority of all \(3^h\) leaves.

A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a leaf-coordinate index \(i\in\{1,\ldots,3^h\}\), its outgoing edges are labeled zero and one, and each terminal node is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), querying a node reveals exactly \(x_i\), costs one unit, and selects the correspondingly labeled edge. Every reachable terminal node must output \(M_h(x)\). One may query coordinates from different subtrees in any order and interleave their evaluation arbitrarily. No requirement to finish one subtree before beginning another is imposed.

Only queries to individual leaf bits are available. Querying an internal majority value, the parity of a set of bits, or a linear combination of bits is not a unit-cost operation. All calculations based on already revealed bits, storage, random sampling and the description of the decision tree are free in this query model. It is a classical model, with no quantum queries. Repeated queries can be answered from the previous reply and removed without increasing cost, so it is harmless to require no repeated coordinate along a path. All such trees have depth at most \(3^h\), and there are finitely many of them for each fixed height.

A randomized decision tree is an input-independent probability distribution \(\mu\) on deterministic trees that each compute the whole function correctly. Its probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, all nonnegative and summing to one. Sampling a tree at the start is equivalent to making random adaptive choices during execution: the algorithm's random choices can be fixed in advance to determine a tree. Zero error requires correctness for every input and every tree assigned positive probability, with no allowed failure output. Since the family of input strings is finite, the almost-sure correctness convention gives the same quantity.

The cost on a fixed input is \(\mathbb E_{T\sim\mu}q_T(x)\). The maximum over \(x\) is taken after these expectations, not inside the expectation. Thus \(Q(h)\) differs from both the uniform-input average cost and the worst query count over all random outcomes. It is also different from bounded-error randomized query complexity, where the output may be wrong with some fixed probability. The minimization over a finite probability simplex attains its value, so \(Q(h)\) is a finite real number; in particular \(Q(0)=1\).

The optimization is performed separately for every height. No bound on the time or description size needed to specify the distribution is part of this model; in particular, no polynomial-time uniform construction of the optimal decision trees is demanded. Both the upper-bound algorithm and the lower bound must address all input strings. An algorithm restricted to a particular traversal order does not define the optimum in this card.

To determine the asymptotic complexity, supply a positive comparison function \(g\) on the nonnegative integers and prove that there are constants \(c,C>0\) and an integer \(h_0\) such that
\[c\,g(h)\le Q(h)\le C\,g(h)\quad\text{for every integer }h\ge h_0.\]
The constants are independent of \(h\). An equivalent statement in the leaf count \(n=3^h\) is acceptable on that domain. A mathematical expression or independently characterized rate may specify \(g\); simply renaming the minimization that defines \(Q\) is not a determination of its growth.

In particular, knowing only a limiting base \(\alpha=\lim_{h\to\infty}Q(h)^{1/h}\) or an exponent \(\log_3\alpha\) need not yield constant-factor bounds on \(Q(h)\): subexponential factors in \(h\) can still matter. Approximating \(\alpha\) within a fixed additive tolerance is weaker still, since distinct fixed bases differ exponentially after raising them to the power \(h\). The requested precision is asymptotic order up to constant factors, not absolute numerical error.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked determination of a positive asymptotic comparison function \(g(h)\), with upper and lower bounds matching up to constants for all sufficiently large integer heights. The upper bound must establish the existence of valid zero-error randomized decision trees with the stated worst-input expected query cost, and the lower bound must hold against every distribution on valid decision trees. It must account for arbitrary adaptive query orders and interleaving. Bounds with different exponential bases, a limiting exponent alone, experiments on finitely many heights, an average-input bound or a lower bound only for restricted traversal algorithms do not settle the target. No efficient uniform algorithm construction is additionally required. The default absolute \(1/100\) tolerance is not applied to this asymptotic complexity target.

source_formulation.text: In Example 8.64, O’Donnell identifies estimating the zero-error randomized decision-tree complexity of recursively composed majority-of-three as a well-studied open problem. Definition 8.61 measures the maximum, over inputs, of the expected number of queries.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Example 8.64 and Definition 8.61; the source’s zero-error model is retained and asymptotic acceptance requires matching constant factors

context_blocks.text: Recursive majority is a small, symmetric rule repeated through a deep tree. Although the rule is simple, choosing which leaf values to reveal can exploit information collected in distant parts of the tree. This makes the family a basic test case for the power of adaptive randomization in exact function evaluation.

The deterministic query complexity is \(3^h\), whereas the book records a zero-error upper bound \((8/3)^h\). Thus randomization saves a polynomial factor in the number of leaves even though the algorithm must never make a mistake. The book explicitly notes that this elementary bound is not optimal.

Magniez and coauthors give the upper bound \(Q(h)\le 1.007\cdot 2.64944^h\), as well as improved lower bounds. The journal article appeared online in 2015 and in the 2016 volume; its full author version provides the precise expected-query model and constants.

Göös and Jayram prove a stronger lower bound for bounded-error randomized decision trees, stated in particular as \(\Omega(2.59^h)\). It also lower-bounds the present zero-error expected-cost model up to a constant factor. Their more precise exponential base is \((35/2)^{1/3}\), with a logarithmic loss in converting their theorem to constant-error queries; the lower and upper exponential rates still do not match.

Al-Dhalaan and Ben-David’s 2026 work equates the zero-error and bounded-error composition limits for recursive majority. These limits describe the bases of exponential growth as height increases. The same work explicitly says that their value remains unknown; equality of these limits does not supply matching constant-factor bounds for the query-complexity function on this card.

The source separately discusses average cost under uniformly random inputs. That quantity is not the minimax expected cost retained here. Likewise, results for parity-query trees or quantum algorithms use different access to the input and cannot be substituted for the requested model.
